    Rainbow Trader Rule-Based Engine Expansion Audit and Research Direction

    Executive conclusion

    Rainbow Trader can become much more expressive without being redesigned if you keep the current split architecture and make the rule path deeper rather than broader. The highest-value direction is not “build a generic trading platform.” It is: keep the existing deterministic model → bot → risk → backtest flow, make the model-side rule language richer, then add a second, position-aware bot-side rule evaluator that emits a small declarative action object which the existing bot, risk manager, and backtester validate and execute. That direction is already compatible with what the selected code visibly does today: the bot is already separated from risk sizing, the backtester already consumes structured orders, and trailing-stop state is already applied and persisted in the live simulation loop. fileciteturn3file1L37-L44 fileciteturn6file1L531-L612 fileciteturn5file1L160-L172

    The most important architectural finding from the repos I could directly inspect is that the current internal plan is directionally right but already stale in at least one important place: the plan treats trailing-stop behavior as a known defect to fix, but the currently selected bot-logic and backtesting-engine code already contain a pure trailing-stop updater, apply it before exit checks, persist the changed stop state, and label stop exits as TRAILING_STOP when appropriate. That means the right first move is not to redesign trailing; it is to lock the current behavior down with tests and treat it as an invariant before extending rule expressiveness further. fileciteturn2file1L261-L270 fileciteturn4file0L5-L10 fileciteturn4file0L142-L230 fileciteturn4file0L230-L307 fileciteturn6file1L531-L558

    The strongest minimal expansion is this:

    • keep canonical feature keys as they already are;
    • keep single-slot references;
    • add continuous ranges and comma-separated disjoint ranges inside the same access syntax;
    • add a small whitelist of safe window and event functions;
    • expose much more of the existing feature infrastructure to rule experiments;
    • add a bot-rule stage that can say not only “open” or “close,” but also “add,” “reduce,” “move stop,” “move TP,” and “enable/update trailing,” while leaving execution semantics to the current bot/risk/backtest layers. fileciteturn9file1L453-L512 fileciteturn9file1L2197-L2353 fileciteturn3file1L424-L639 fileciteturn5file1L160-L172

    The research literature and platform survey both point the same way: the most robust and transferable deterministic strategy families are still trend/trend-following, time-series momentum, breakout, and simple regime-filtered pullback systems; mean-reversion and spread systems are still useful, but they are materially more fragile to costs, timing, and execution details. In crypto specifically, long-horizon trend-following remains one of the more defensible deterministic families in the published literature, while short-horizon or heavily tuned mean-reversion is much easier to overfit. citeturn14academia0turn14academia3turn11view2turn16academia2

    One access limitation matters. I could directly inspect the main repo, the current plan, the generator, bot-logic, backtesting-engine, and module READMEs that define the monorepo shape, but I could not directly inspect the model-trainer, common, or database submodule code through the currently enabled repo/tool set in this run. So the model-DSL parser / AST / evaluator details below are split into code-verified findings and plan-derived findings rather than being presented as fully verified end to end.     What other serious trading systems teach without forcing a redesign

    Other mature systems converge on a few design ideas that matter for Rainbow Trader.

    TradingView Pine Script centers strategy logic on time series. It uses the [] history operator for past values, treats higher/lower timeframe access as explicit request.*() operations, and treats lower-timeframe requests as arrays because multiple lower-timeframe bars can exist inside one chart bar. Its strategy layer can place, modify, and cancel hypothetical orders and exposes entries, exits, pyramiding, slippage, and other backtest settings. The useful lesson for Rainbow is not “become Pine.” The useful lesson is: keep history access first-class, keep cross-timeframe access explicit, and keep repaint / synthetic-price / timeframe-alignment semantics explicit. citeturn5view0turn5view1turn5view2turn20view0

    Backtrader uses a very compact bar-indexing model: 0 is the current bar, -1 the previous one, then -2, -3, and so on. It also distinguishes single-value indexing from pulling a backward-looking slice through get(ago=..., size=...), and it explicitly documents that differing timeframes require coupling machinery. That is extremely close to the mental model you already want. The part Rainbow should learn is the clarity of the indexing contract, not the unrestricted Python callback model. citeturn18view0turn18view1turn18view2

    QuantConnect LEAN makes indicator creation, readiness, warm-up, and history requests explicit. It supports automatic indicators tied to subscriptions, manual indicators, fixed warm-up periods, and multi-asset trailing history requests. That is important for Rainbow because your rule battalion will live or die on feature availability, warm-up correctness, and MTF / multi-symbol history semantics. LEAN’s strongest lesson is that indicator readiness and history access should be explicit contracts, not hidden conveniences. citeturn6view1turn6view2turn6view3

    vectorbt is valuable because of how cleanly it separates signal simulation, order simulation, and analysis. Its Portfolio.from_signals() interface also shows that once you move from bare entries/exits to real strategy management, you quickly need explicit handling of long/short conflicts, opposite-entry behavior, partial sizing, stop-loss, trailing stops, take-profit, and stop-update hooks. Rainbow should not copy vectorbt’s vectorized API surface verbatim, but it should copy the conceptual separation: signals are not orders, and orders are not performance metrics. citeturn19view1turn19view0

    Freqtrade is the closest external confirmation of your two-stage idea. It exposes strategy callbacks for custom_exit(), custom_stoploss(), and adjust_trade_position(), and those callbacks receive trade state such as the open trade, current price, current profit, leverage, prior fills, and dataframe-derived indicators. It also supports partial exits, additional entries, dynamic stoploss changes, and post-fill callbacks. Rainbow should not import Freqtrade’s whole callback architecture, but it should absolutely learn from the fact that serious standalone strategies need a state-aware management layer after entry, not just a directional classifier. citeturn5view7turn5view8turn21view0turn21view1turn21view2

    TradeStation EasyLanguage is useful for one specific reason: it formalizes protective management primitives as first-class strategy semantics. SetStopLoss and SetProfitTarget are not treated as incidental arithmetic; they are dedicated strategy constructs, and the docs explicitly note that these can behave differently from normal “next bar” order generation because they enable same-bar protective logic. The right Rainbow takeaway is not to add EasyLanguage reserved words; it is to recognize that entry logic and protective-order semantics are not the same layer and sometimes need a dedicated contract. citeturn19view2turn19view3

    AmiBroker provides a warning that maps almost perfectly to your MTF concerns: arrays live on timelines, and once you compress to another timeframe you must explicitly expand or realign before using the result on the original timeframe. That is exactly why your future range/index DSL must be strict about what sequence is being indexed and how slower features are aligned at decision time. citeturn9view7turn9view8

    NautilusTrader shows the virtue of explicit separation between configuration and mutable strategy state, and of using the same strategy source for backtest and live trading. That is consistent with your current goal: keep Rainbow’s architecture intact, then enrich the contracts between layers rather than hiding more logic inside one giant monolithic DSL. citeturn9view2

    The common lesson across all of them is simple. Mature platforms give the user one or more of these: history access, explicit time alignment, stateful management hooks, and a clear distinction between signal generation and order management. The main thing they do that Rainbow should not copy is unrestricted general-purpose scripting. That would immediately trade away determinism, auditability, and safe experiment generation for flexibility you do not need in phase one. citeturn5view0turn6view2turn19view0turn21view0turn9view2

    The five highest-value deterministic strategy families for the first Rainbow strategy catalog

    The evidence base does not say that every classic technical strategy still makes money after costs. It does say something narrower and more useful: the most defensible families for a first serious deterministic catalog are the ones with a stable behavioral or structural rationale, transferable definitions, and relatively modest parameter counts. In practice, that points to five anchor families.

    Multi-timeframe breakout and trend-following. This is the cleanest first family. It includes Donchian/Turtle-like highest-high breakouts, channel breakouts, and moving-average breakout variants, then manages risk with ATR or structure-based stops and, optionally, pyramids only after favorable movement. Very long-run evidence for trend following remains strong across asset classes, and crypto-specific evidence is much better for trend following than many people assume. For Rainbow, this family fits naturally once you can express max(high over window), min(low over window), cross above breakout level, and bot-stage actions for “add” and “move stop.” citeturn14academia0turn14academia3

    Time-series momentum with regime filters. This is not the same as a simple breakout, although the implementations often overlap. The core is sign or strength of past return over one or more horizons, optionally volatility-normalized, plus a regime veto such as volatility too high, market breadth bad, or a contextual symbol risk-off filter. This family is academically stronger than most indicator folklore, and it transfers well to crypto because it requires very little market microstructure sophistication. In Rainbow it needs past-return or log-return features, window aggregations, and multi-symbol context exposure, but not a portfolio engine if you trade one base symbol at a time. citeturn14academia0turn11view2turn14academia3turn10academia3

    Trend-filtered pullback and mean reversion. This is the family where RSI, Bollinger-style distance from average, z-score pullbacks, and “revert to moving average only when higher-timeframe trend is aligned” belong. The literature and replications are much more fragile here: mean-reversion systems can look fantastic on benchmark datasets and fall apart after realistic costs or when recent market structure shifts. That makes them good catalog candidates, but bad candidates for naive parameter mining. In Rainbow they fit well if you expose enough raw semantic features and support avg, std, zscore-like precomputed features, persistence, and exit-on-recovery rules. citeturn16academia2

    Intermarket and relative-strength confirmation. This family uses other symbols as context rather than as co-executed positions: for example, “trade ETH long only if BTC daily trend is positive and BTC volatility is below threshold,” or “take alt breakout only if BTC dominance or market proxy is not deteriorating.” This family is especially attractive for Rainbow because it leverages your existing multi-symbol / multi-timeframe feature generation idea without forcing an immediate move to shared-portfolio execution. It is also one of the best ways to make a deterministic engine expressive enough to detect regime and context without model training. fileciteturn9file1L420-L512 citeturn5view1turn6view3

    Spread and pairs mean reversion. Conceptually this is still a major quant family: define a spread or ratio, normalize it, enter when the deviation is extreme, exit when it reverts or the spread regime breaks. But this is the first family where the “fits / does not fit” line matters. If you precompute a spread or z-score feature and use it only to decide one-symbol execution, Rainbow can represent a lot of the logic. If you want true market-neutral two-leg execution with entries, exits, slippage, and sizing on both legs inside one shared portfolio, that is a larger capability. So this family is the best example of a strategy that is partly representable now, partly beyond first-phase scope. citeturn16academia1turn12academia1

    If the question is “which families are most worth betting the first major deterministic battalion on,” the answer is not symmetric. The strongest first bet is still trend / breakout / time-series momentum, followed by trend-filtered pullback systems and intermarket confirmation, with spread / two-leg stat-arb as a partially deferred family. That hierarchy is supported both by the published evidence and by how naturally each family fits your current architecture. citeturn14academia0turn14academia3turn11view2turn16academia2

    Which capabilities fit your target engine naturally and which do not

    Your preferred hybrid model is the right one. A market-rule evaluator should remain responsible for market interpretation: long, short, none, optional regime tag, optional matched-rule ID, and maybe optional strength/quality overrides if they have a concrete consumer. A bot-rule evaluator should then be responsible for state-aware management: veto entry, delay entry, add, reduce, close, reverse as a macro, move stop, move TP, enable/update trailing, and force-flat. That is exactly the split that your current code already hints at: the bot generates proposals, the risk manager approves/rejects them, and the backtester executes structured orders later. fileciteturn3file1L37-L44 fileciteturn3file1L424-L779 fileciteturn6file1L559-L612

    The minimal temporal model should stay very close to the current conceptual syntax rather than inventing an alien rule language. The best recommendation is:

    • keep single offsets like feature{-1} and feature{-7};
    • add continuous windows like feature{-20:-1};
    • add disjoint windows like feature{-60:-50,-20:-1};
    • reject positive offsets;
    • keep indexing relative to the feature’s own aligned sequence, which is exactly what you wanted. fileciteturn2file1L47-L54 fileciteturn9file1L453-L512

    I would not make the first expansion a full Pine-style series algebra. The safe compromise is better: window selectors can produce an internal series-like selection that is legal only inside a whitelist of deterministic functions. In practice that means functions such as avg, sum, min, max, count_true, any_true, all_true, first, last, change, pct_change, std, bars_since, cross_up, and cross_down. Heavier or repeatedly reused things such as z-score, correlations, spreads, volatility-normalized transforms, and cross-symbol ratios should usually live in the feature layer, because Rainbow already has a deterministic data-processing module and generator infrastructure for precomputing and naming features cleanly. fileciteturn7file0L50-L75 fileciteturn9file1L2197-L2353 citeturn6view2turn19view1

    The natural fit categories look like this.

    Fits the target engine with small extensions: breakout systems, moving-average systems, RSI/Bollinger pullbacks, regime filters, intermarket confirmation, ATR-based exits, break-even rules, trailing activation, delayed trailing, signal deterioration exits, cooldowns, bars-since-entry, and pyramiding where additions are same-symbol and position-aware. These all sit comfortably inside a richer model DSL plus a state-aware bot-rule layer. fileciteturn3file1L424-L779 fileciteturn4file0L142-L307 citeturn21view0turn21view1

    Fits after one larger but still coherent extension: expression-level window predicates, because serious strategies often need statements like “condition A was true in at least 12 of the last 20 bars” or “cross occurred once in the last 15 bars.” This is still reasonable, but it should be implemented through a small internal series/predicate abstraction, not through arbitrary loops or list comprehensions. Pine, Backtrader, and vectorbt all show why expression-over-series is useful; your safe AST model shows why it should stay constrained. citeturn5view0turn18view1turn19view0

    Requires a larger deferred capability: true cross-sectional momentum, ranking, and portfolio allocation across many simultaneously tradable symbols with shared capital, turnover control, and rebalancing. That is a portfolio engine problem, not just a prettier rule DSL problem. LEAN, vectorbt, and Nautilus can do this because they are explicit multi-asset engines. Rainbow should learn from them eventually, but not in the first rule-engine expansion. citeturn6view3turn19view1turn9view2

    Outside the natural first-phase scope: market making, order-book imbalance systems, sub-bar microstructure execution, options surface strategies, or generalized scriptable state machines with arbitrary mutable state and loops. Those require either intrabar event streams, a different execution simulator, or a much more general programming environment than the one you want. citeturn5view2turn20view0turn9view2

    The minimal expansion plan that unlocks the most strategy coverage

    The first recommendation is to treat the present system as a set of seams to extend, not as something to bulldoze. The best seam is the one you were already pointing at.

    First, widen feature exposure rather than inventing a new engine. The code already shows that general feature generation can span multiple timeframes and named indicator variants, while rule_raw is the thin bottleneck. So phase one should make far more of the existing feature universe selectable for deterministic strategies, with canonical names preserved, instead of forcing a second naming convention or an alternate data path. That gives you immediate access to MTF, multi-symbol, raw OHLCV-derived columns, and many more indicators with minimal architectural damage. fileciteturn9file1L2353-L2429 fileciteturn7file0L52-L75

    Second, extend the rule selector syntax, not the whole programming model. The smallest coherent jump is from single offsets to richer selectors: {-n}, {-a:-b}, and comma-separated disjoint ranges. That is the extension most aligned with what you asked for, the current June plan, and the way serious systems think about history access. If parser ambiguity appears in the actual model-trainer code, the fallback should be a helper form, not a new DSL philosophy. But the first attempt should absolutely stay close to the current braces model because that preserves continuity with your existing mental model and existing research notes. fileciteturn2file1L47-L54 citeturn18view0turn5view0

    Third, add only a small evaluator whitelist. In the evaluator itself, I would keep only cheap, deterministic, auditable primitives: arithmetic, comparisons, boolean operators, abs, min, max, contiguous/disjoint window aggregates, and event helpers like cross_up, cross_down, bars_since, count_true, and consecutive_true. Anything expensive, repeated, or ambiguous should be precomputed as features. That division matches both Rainbow’s current data-processing architecture and what mature systems do in practice: indicator computation lives in a feature layer, while rules combine already aligned series and a narrow set of safe transforms. fileciteturn7file0L52-L75 citeturn6view2turn19view0

    Fourth, add a minimal bot action object instead of trying to cram all management into the model output. The current bot already creates entry proposals with stop-loss, take-profit, trailing activation, and trailing distance, and the backtester already knows how to execute structured OPEN and CLOSE orders. The next step is to add a thin declarative layer with fields like intent, side, size_delta, close_fraction, stop_loss, take_profit, trailing_activation, trailing_distance, and reason_code. Then let the existing bot/risk/backtest code translate that into concrete orders. That matches your stated goal almost exactly while preserving Rainbow’s current split responsibilities. fileciteturn3file1L424-L779 fileciteturn5file1L160-L172 citeturn21view0turn21view1

    Fifth, defer true portfolio logic. Context symbols and one-base-symbol-per-experiment are enough to unlock a surprisingly large strategy catalog. Relative strength filters, risk-on/risk-off market gating, BTC-leading-ETH context, volatility vetoes, and cross-market confirmation can all be modeled without immediately building a shared portfolio allocator. The moment you need cross-sectional ranks, top-k selection, rebalance scheduling, and simultaneous capital competition across many open symbols, you are in another project. fileciteturn9file1L420-L512 citeturn6view3turn19view1

    Validation method and what should happen next in the research line

    The June 16 plan is very good on methodology, and on this point I would keep its spirit almost unchanged. It recommends a separate lab structure for rule-based research, one experiment per strategy to avoid shadowing, and a chronological split where development happens on earlier data, validation later, and 2026 is preserved as a true later test period rather than being repeatedly reused for tuning. It also correctly emphasizes a control battery before scaling the battalion and warns that multiple-testing control matters once the search gets large. That is all still the right direction. fileciteturn2file1L261-L302

    What I would add is a stricter experiment ledger. Every deterministic experiment should record at least: strategy family, base logic ID, parameter variant, feature profile, symbol context profile, execution profile, and source hypothesis. If you later want honest robustness scoring, you need a durable record of the whole tested family, not just the winners. That is exactly the sort of battalion discipline that keeps a powerful rule engine from becoming a brute-force overfitting machine. The deflated-Sharpe / backtest-overfitting literature exists for exactly this reason: once you run many correlated trials, the best historical curve is no longer a reliable estimate of real skill. fileciteturn2file1L281-L294 citeturn22search0

    The metric set should also remain broader than net PnL: return, drawdown, exposure, turnover, trade frequency, profitability across folds, profitability across assets, friction retention, and stability across neighboring parameter settings. That is not academic ceremony; it is the only way to stop the rule battalion from selecting noisy, brittle strategies whose attractive curve comes from one narrow period or one lucky market regime. The current plan already points in that direction, and the external platforms reinforce it by exposing detailed order records, trade lists, and performance decompositions rather than one top-line return number. fileciteturn2file1L281-L294 citeturn20view0turn19view1

    On the X-profile side, I did attempt to inspect the public profile you linked, but in this environment the page rendered as an unreadable shell and I did not obtain materially usable post content from it. So, in this run, the X profile did not materially affect the conclusions, and the conclusions above are driven by the GitHub code and primary external documentation rather than social posts. citeturn0view0

    Netting it all out, the most accurate condensed recommendation is this:

    Rainbow Trader should become a hybrid deterministic strategy system built from two evaluators. The first evaluator reads canonical Rainbow features and produces a market interpretation. The second evaluator reads that interpretation plus current position state and emits a declarative management action. The surrounding architecture stays Rainbow: bot, risk manager, and backtester remain the execution authority. The first five strategy families to codify should be breakout/trend-following, time-series momentum, trend-filtered pullback mean reversion, intermarket confirmation, and spread/pairs logic with the explicit note that true two-leg execution is a later capability. That path gives you the biggest possible jump in real strategy expressiveness for the smallest coherent architectural change. fileciteturn3file1L37-L44 fileciteturn6file1L559-L612 citeturn14academia0turn14academia3turn16academia2turn12academia1
